newsitem.title: ANGOLA: Diana earns only praise in Angola for mine crusade.
newsitem.headline: Diana earns only praise in Angola for mine crusade.

text.p: Britain's Princess Diana may have sparked a row at home over her support for a campaign to ban landmines, but she has earned only praise from the people she met in war-riven Angola.
Her four-day visit as a volunteer for the British Red Cross, which launched the campaign and invited her to see one of the world's most heavily-mined countries, has been a personal victory.

The 35-year-old mother of two has managed to carve herself a new role, for which she has long searched and which she is clearly comfortable with. She now hopes to visit troublespots around the globe such as Bosnia, Afghanistan and Cambodia.
Diana obviously liked the informality of the visit which saw her cast aside her glamorous image for jeans and sneakers.
It was her first working trip abroad since her divorce last year from heir to the throne Prince Charles.
It was also one of the most sombre overseas visits she has undertaken: she chatted to children and adults maimed by landmines and even saw landmine victims with their stomachs blown out.

"What I would like to see is for Princess Diana to become the ambassador of all the de-miners in the world," Peter Isaacs, chief of the United Nations demining programme in Angola, told Reuters after meeting Diana.
"In that way there may be pressure on governments -- particularly Western governments and indeed international corporations -- to come up with money (for demining)," he added.

Isaacs, a landmine victim himself, said the princess' visit could not have been more timely for Angola as the U.N. was about to launch an appeal for $25 million to cover demining operations in the country for 1997.

Ordinary Angolans, surprised by the visit of a princess who is relatively unknown in the southern Africa country, nicknamed Diana the "princess of peace" as she toured health posts and orthopaedic centres in slums around the capital Luanda and in two of its most war-devastated towns, Kuito and Huambo.
The Angolan government, participating in a peace plan with the former rebel UNITA movement to end nearly two decades of civil war, invited the princess to return to Luanda.

"I hope the princess will visit us again. We want to thank her for taking the time off to come and help," Angola's Foreign Minister Venancio de Moura told a small gathering shortly before Diana left Angola on Thursday.

"This visit has been a help to the process which we are going through, but especially for the children and people of Angola. She has visited some parts (of the country) that we consider important and most affected by the war," he said.

Diana brushed aside as "merely a distraction" critics in Britain who said she was meddling in politics by supporting the landmine ban. "I am not a political figure, the fact is I am a humanitarian figure and always will be," she told reporters.

"I think this is what Angola needed. This has definitely been helpful to the country and to the confidence of its people," said Francois de la Roche of the International Federation of the Red Cross in Angola.

Head of the International Committee of the Red Cross in Angola, Michel Dufour, praised Diana's crusade against landmines as an inspiration for its victims. Angola has the world's highest amputee rate at three per thousand people.
Dufour told Reuters: "The visit has given more visibility to the campaign and for the victims of landmines, it has been a light in the darkness."
